newsitem.title: USA: TV journalist Brinkley apologizes to Clinton.
newsitem.headline: TV journalist Brinkley apologizes to Clinton.

text.p: Veteran TV journalist David Brinkley apologised to President Bill Clinton in a programme broadcast on Sunday for having called him "a bore" while on the air election night.

Brinkley, 76, offered the apology at the start of a half-hour interview with the president that marked the journalist's retirement as host of his "This Week with David Brinkley" news analysis show after 15 years.
"Before we begin I am reminded of something I wrote years ago," Brinkley said. "It may be impossible to be objective, I said, but we must always be fair."

"Well, after a long day -- election day -- and seven hours on the set, what I said at the end of our election night coverage was both impolite and unfair. And I'm sorry. I regret it," Brinkley told Clinton.
Clinton, who taped the interview on Friday in the White House Roosevelt Room, immediately accepted the apology.
"Let me just say, I accept that. I've said a lot of things myself late at night when I was tired and you had really been through a rough day," Clinton said.
"I always believe you have to judge people on their whole work. And if you get judged based on your whole work, you come out way ahead," the president added.
Brinkley, who will continue to work as a commentator on the programme, had hoped that the interview with Clinton would be a highlight of his move into semi-retirement.
But he cast a pall over his departure this week as host of the programme by slamming Clinton in his final summation during the wrap-up of ABC's live coverange on November 5, election night.
Brinkley complimented his colleagues on their creativity, but said "Clinton ... has not a creative bone in his body. Therefore he is a bore and will always be a bore."
That came on top on his predicting that the second Clinton administration will be "four more years ... of nonsense" and calling Clinton's victory statement "one of the worst things I've ever heard."
Clinton joked in the interview that Brinkley's remarks had pleased one person at the White House, Vice President Al Gore, who has a reputation as a dull and wooden speaker.
"One person loved it," Clinton said. "The vice president was very happy."
